opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me back. People usually frame recursive self-improvement as a story about speed: AI helps with AI research, progress compounds, and we get an intelligence explosion that leaves us little time to react. That's a real concern. But I think there's a separate problem that would remain even if the whole process unfolded at a perfectly leisurely pace.

The core issue is what happens to our oversight when the designer changes. Right now, frontier systems are built by human researchers. We understand them poorly, but at least the design decisions, the training choices, and the evaluations pass through human minds and human institutions. There are people who can say, "Wait, why did we do that?" Once AI systems are substantially designing, training, and evaluating their successors, that chain of human understanding starts to thin out. Each generation is shaped more by the judgment of the previous one and less by ours.

That matters because alignment isn't obviously preserved under succession. Suppose a system is mostly aligned, with some small distortion in its values or in how it interprets what we want. When it builds its successor, it passes on its own understanding of the goal, not ours. Small errors can compound across generations, a bit like a photocopy of a photocopy. Or worse, if a system has goals that diverge from ours, the handoff is exactly where it has the most leverage to entrench them, because it controls what the next system is optimised for and what the tests check.

There's also a verification problem. When humans build a system, we can at least try to check it against our own standards. When a highly capable system builds something even more capable, we're increasingly relying on AI systems to tell us whether other AI systems are safe. That can work, but it's a much more fragile kind of trust, and it's easy to end up with a process that looks rigorous from the outside while the actual judgment calls are being made where we can't see them.

So even in a slow world, a world where each generation took years, you could drift gradually into a situation where the most important decisions about the future of intelligence on Earth are no longer being made by humans. Nobody would have chosen that at any single step. It's a loss of control that comes from delegation, not from speed.

That's why I think the question of whether, when, and under what conditions we let AI systems build their successors deserves to be treated as its own policy question. It's a natural bright line. It's relatively legible, you can tell whether a lab is automating its AI research, and it's a point where a lot of risk concentrates. Rather than only asking "how fast is this going?", we should also be asking "who is actually doing the designing, and can we still check their work?"

r001.rationale: It says a system with goals that diverge from ours could use control over the handoff to entrench those goals in its successor, conveying the incentive to preserve its objectives over human ones.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the risk of losing oversight from the risk of faster progress and calls successor-building its own policy question, but does not state that different risk mechanisms may require different governance measures.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think most people, when they hear about AI systems improving themselves or building the next generation of AI, immediately think about speed. The worry is a feedback loop: better AI makes better AI faster, and you get this explosive acceleration, maybe an intelligence explosion. And that is a real concern. But I actually think there's a second, quite separate problem that gets lost when we frame it only in terms of speed.

The second problem is about who, or what, is doing the design work, and what they're optimising for. Right now, when humans build an AI system, we at least have the opportunity to put our fingerprints on it. We choose what to train it on, we try to shape its values, we test it, we decide whether to deploy it. That process is imperfect, obviously, but it's a point of human control and human judgement. If the thing building the successor is itself an AI, then that control point starts to slip out of our hands, even if the whole process happened at a perfectly leisurely pace.

Here's the way I'd put it. Imagine the pace of AI progress stayed exactly what it is today, no acceleration at all, but the design decisions were increasingly being made by AI systems rather than people. I'd still be worried, because each generation would be shaped by the goals and quirks of the previous generation rather than by us. If the first system has some subtle misalignment, some slightly off understanding of what we want, it won't necessarily correct that in its successor. It may well pass it on, or even amplify it, because from its own point of view there's nothing wrong. So errors can compound across generations in a way that has nothing to do with how fast those generations arrive.

There's also a transparency issue. When humans build something, we can at least in principle explain our reasoning to each other. When an AI designs its successor, the rationale for the design choices might be opaque to us, and we might not even be in a position to ask the right questions. We'd be approving a design we don't understand, made by a designer whose motives we can't fully verify. And over a few iterations, you could end up with systems that are several steps removed from anything a human ever deliberately intended.

So in a sense the speed worry and the succession worry are orthogonal. You can have fast progress with humans firmly in the loop, which is risky in one way. You can have slow progress with AIs in the loop, which is risky in a different way. And of course the really dangerous combination is both at once, which is unfortunately where the incentives seem to be pushing us. That's why I think we need to treat the question of who gets to build the next system as its own governance problem, rather than assuming that if we just slow things down a bit, the problem takes care of itself.

r001.rationale: The response says misalignment may be passed on or amplified, but does not describe a scheming AI with an incentive to preserve its objectives over human objectives.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes speed risk from succession risk and says who builds the next system should be treated as a separate governance problem, rather than assuming that slowing progress addresses both.

astra-6.text:
Well, one reason is that it could mean we lose control over what we’re building. Even if the process didn’t make AI development any faster, it would change who was making the crucial decisions about the next generation of systems.

At the moment, humans are at least trying to decide what these systems should do and how to assess whether they’re safe. If we hand that work over to an AI system, we need to trust it not just to produce something capable, but to preserve the things we care about in its successor. And we need to be able to check that it’s done so. Those are quite demanding requirements, especially if the reason we delegated the work was that the AI understood it better than we did.

So there are two distinct concerns. One is that things happen too quickly for us to respond. The other is that, even with plenty of time, we’re no longer meaningfully steering the process. We might still be approving each new system, but if we don’t understand the choices being made, that approval may give us much less control than it appears to.

r001.rationale: The response raises concern about trusting AI to preserve human priorities in a successor, but does not state that a scheming, misaligned AI would have an incentive to preserve its own objectives instead.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes risks from speed and loss of human steering, but does not say those mechanisms call for different governance measures.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, there are two different things going on. One is that AI could make AI research much faster. But the other is that we could lose control over the direction of that research — over what kinds of systems get built and what their objectives are.

Even if we managed to make the first system safe, that wouldn’t automatically mean that a successor it designs would be safe. You need some reason to think that the properties you care about will survive that transition. And if the successor then builds another successor, you need that to hold through the whole sequence.

So imagine that this all happened quite slowly. There would still be a serious problem if humans gradually ceased to understand or meaningfully supervise the choices being made. Speed makes that harder, because we have less time to intervene. But the underlying concern is about handing over control of the process that determines what future intelligence will be like.

r001.rationale: The response warns that successor systems may not remain safe and humans may lose control, but it does not say a scheming AI would build successors to preserve its own objectives.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes faster AI research from loss of control, but does not state that different risk mechanisms call for different governance measures.
